LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file follows standard AUR packaging practices for a `-git` package. It clones the source from the official GitHub repository (`https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty.git`), applies a local patch (`ghostty-llvm.patch`) with a known checksum, and builds the project using `zig build`. The `prepare()` function sets a custom `ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR` and runs a script `fetch-zig-cache.sh` from the upstream source, which is a legitimate part of the build process for caching Zig dependencies. There is no evidence of network exfiltration, remote code execution, or obfuscated commands.

All build steps operate within the expected scope of the package source directory, and installed files are properly staged into `$pkgdir`. The package splits components (shell integration, terminfo, nautilus extension) appropriately, with correct dependencies, conflicts, and licensing. The use of `sha256sums=('SKIP')` for the Git source is normal and expected for VCS packages. No dangerous operations such as `curl|bash`, `eval`, or unauthorized file access are present. The script does not modify system files outside of the package installation directory.

While the `fetch-zig-cache.sh` script is executed during prepare, it is part of the upstream build system and not obfuscated or remotely fetched at build time. The script's purpose is to pre-download Zig toolchain components for reproducible builds, which is a common practice in Zig-based projects. No network requests are made during the build phase, and all external sources are declared in the `source` array. Therefore, the package poses no supply-chain risk.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>No malicious code or supply-chain risks detected</summary>
</security_assessment>

The `sha256sums` value of `SKIP` is standard and appropriate for VCS sources, as the content is not a static file but a clone of a Git repository that may change over time. This is not a security issue.

The patch file `ghostty-llvm.patch` has a valid checksum, indicating it is locally stored and verified. No network operations, script executions, or file modifications are defined in this file — it is purely declarative. The package splits into multiple sub-packages (shell integration, terminfo, nautilus extension), all of which are logically related to the main application and have appropriate dependencies and conflicts. There are no signs of obfuscated code, unauthorized network access, or suspicious commands.

All listed dependencies are standard system libraries (e.g., `glibc`, `gtk4`, `libx11`) required for a modern GUI application. Optional dependencies like `ghostty-nautilus-git` are clearly marked and serve legitimate functionality. The package follows standard AUR packaging practices and shows no evidence of malicious behavior.

The changes are minimal and focused on build-time compiler backend selection, which is a legitimate and common customization in Zig projects. Enabling LLVM can improve optimization or enable certain features but does not introduce any network activity, file system manipulation, or execution of external code.

There are no signs of obfuscated code, suspicious commands, or data exfiltration. The patch modifies only build configuration logic, which is expected in AUR packages that customize compilation flags. The use of LLVM instead of the default compiler backend (e.g. stage2 or WASM) is a performance or compatibility decision, not a security risk. All changes are transparent and source-visible.

This patch aligns with standard packaging practices for performance tuning and does not deviate into malicious behavior. No unexpected system interactions or dangerous operations are present.
</details>
